title: Dan Norder: Chase: The BASIC Language Proto-Roguelike
speaker: Dan Norder
description: In the early years of computing, a small turn-based game called Chase, built in the BASIC programming language, had players escaping robots and luring them into obstacles. It soon developed variations and enhancements as it spread to other computer systems. On the 60th anniversary of BASIC, we will examine these "robotlike" games and how the gameplay might be used in modern roguelikes.

segments.text: Our final talk is from Dan Norder. A computer hobbyist for more than 45 years, I got started
with roguelike games in 1987 with one of the first versions of NetHack. In the '90s I focused
on desktop publishing and then combined those skills and Internet experience into a professional
career. I'm currently working on a retro 8-bit pixel art roguelike game project, Elflings. and
Here celebrate the 50th anniversary of BASIC. DAN: Thank you for having me and staying up for
the last presentation of the evening. This is all about chase which is the BASIC language
proto-roguelike. I have my Mastodon address @elflings which was the game mentioned. What
this presentation is going to be about basically is -- what's this doing? Robots, robots, robots.
We kind of already did an about me so I don't really need to go over this and I will use the
time for the rest of the presentation. All right. When I talk about a proto-roguelike, how is chase
like a primitive roguelike? Well, it is top-down, it is turn-based, and the GIFs here are a symbol
of the location of items. It is not like a text description like you are in a wind of twisty
passage ways. It is showing you a map actually. And the placement of objects are entirely random.
Of course, there is permadeath. Over on the right, I made a screen. The original would be one
color. Black on white for paper for the very first version. I have colorized it to make it stand out
more. You can see that the player is an asterisk which is in green. Robots are the enemy in red
and the X sign. The obstacles are Xs -- plus sign. The player moves one to the right and the robots
just follow after you. One of the five robots is already crashed into an obstacle and died. The
rest are just kind of chasing after you which is where the name comes from. Chase, however, is not
a real roguelike because it is extremely basic. This is just the player, the robots, and the
walls. I explained the entire game. No inventory, skills, stats, no multiple ways to do things which
is one of the coolest things of roguelikes. It is not technically even procedurally based
because the randomness is too random. It just throws everything out there and it lands where
it lands. And most unusual way is there is no real combat at least in the typical sense.
Then we move again here and the player hops up behind an obstacle and two more robots crash and
the remaining two are following after you and they are going crash very soon now. All right. Chase,
you runaway from the enemies, avoid the walls and robots. The walls are electrified fences is what
they decided to call them. Another important thing is that the robots always follow the
shortest passable route to chase you. You can predict exactly where they are going to go. And
if you are lined up with them like you happen to be right now they will come closer. But if
they are diagonal in any way they could take a diagonal route to get to you. All you do is you
avoid getting killed and you want to get the robots to run into the obstacles. That's it.
All right. To understand how this was created, what sort of things are going on at the time,
you also need a little short basic idea of where BASIC came from. BASIC was created at Dartmouth
college by members of the math department, John Kemeny and Thomas Kurtz. John became
the president later of the college. It stands for beginners all purpose symbolic instruction code.
The idea was to be easier than the existing languages at the time that only people into
science and math could figure it out. They integrated it into the Dartmouth timesharing
system. BASIC was created 60 years ago starting in May of 1964 slightly after midnight in fact.
This screen shows you a setup for how the first basic lab was run. Kurtz is in the middle from
the main frame from general electric. Kemeny is on the right. The other photos are computer
labs. BASIC was integrated into the whole college eventually. People in all sorts of
classes were using it. They estimated up to 85% of the students were using it because it was
integrated so well. If you look at the picture, you can see the first terminals were teletype
machines and also one of them has an old phone attached to it. That's how they communicated.
Basically, what you do with the teletypes is you would submit your information in and get
a printout back. Little different than how the screen would update because everything
is printed out for you each time. All the students and professors could use it too would share their
basic programs, adapt code, make improvements, things like that. And Kemeney was forward thinking
believing the games would popularize the language. Of course they did. A lot of people were using it.
This is in contrast to other systems at the time where if they saw you were using up the university
resources to have a game they would delete it. They lost a lot of really good games that way.
Chase was created on this system we believe but don't have a copy of the original so don't have
exact proof. The first indication we can find that chase existed was in creative computing magazine
in the first issue of 1976. You can see from the cover there robots are playing cards with nuts and
bolts and you can see listed on the cover that chase is one of the games. On this version of
Chase was done by Bill Cotter and David Ahl who was the creator of forward thinking. He tried to
credit the original authors but it is listed as unknown here so that's no help. This was created
on the honey well hardware by general electric which was the same hardware that DTSS used which
means this must be close to the original code. In this version, the only choices you had were moving
in one of the eight directions surrounding you. You couldn't teleport which is a major
feature later. You couldn't even wait in place and have the robots chase after you where you
are. You had to move which is a little strange. The next version of chase Herman DeMonstoy. This
was almost the same the only thing was you could choose not to print out a map. The robots were
predictable so you wouldn't necessarily have to print it out. As a comparison, Chase was ported
to assembly language which is a little different than basic. Basic was easier. The code for that
ran about half a page. The assembly language code ran about six pages. It was really hard to figure
out. I don't like assembly. The major change they added was they added the first teleport
already which was hitting the P button for panic. This screenshot is from sole 20 which was a very
early computer. Little joy fish symbol there with the robots in other games. It was like the
ghost and their version of Pacman or a lunar lander. That's in Dr. Dobbs journal in 1977.
1978 we have another example with graphics basic. It includes tub work because that's
popular and add last stand option where you could choose not to move for the entire rest
of the game and hope the robots crash themselves. Killerbot's from Rodger Olsen 1979. Killerbot. You
could deactivate a nuclear bomb. Any way, next up is kind of the major iteration of Chase. It has
all of the features we later know as basically things you could do in chase. It added the
teleport option. It added the stay in place. Added the last stand. Basically it is the chase we know
and love. This was again in creative computing. In 1975. I believe this game was created by Mac
from the next slide. Bill Cotter and further improved by Arnold Leverage when we don't know
is or did. Maybe he did that version of Chase on the previous slide. Everything else is still the
same. That leads us into a very interesting question here. Did Oglesby write Chase?
He wrote a lot of basic games on DTSS starting in 1974 when they loaned him a teletype machine
and phone that connected to the network. He was grateful and decided to help them out and made a
bunch of games. All became convinced that Oglesby created Chase and in a few years he directly
called it his game. Case closed, right? Problem is Oglesby denied creating the game. Said he didn't
create it or port it and just saw it at some point. This is all according to Maury Markowitz.
That's pretty big there. If it was his, he would probably said have he did it. More on this later.
Then we have a new version called Escape for the first time. It is by Jay Victor Nahigian and
William Hodge which came out in 1979 and reprinted in 1980 and '81. This is probably the first
version that didn't have a robot theme. It was based on military combat. It was a lot like chase.
You could only teleport twice. I don't know why. One really new thing is they changed it so that
when the attackers collided they both randomly teleport which I can only imagine was really a
pain. You just spent your time trying to get away and they jump on you or something. And then this
is also important. When you teleport, probably should have mentioned it, teleport goes anywhere.
You could instantly land on one of the obstacles or a robot and die. It wasn't safe. It was just
a last ditch move. And then escape also added a tank which destroyed everything it touched. All
right. Next up, Hi-volts is an interesting one. Kind of like Chase, we don't have a copy of the
original ones. It was created by Douglas Jones and I am guessing 1979, could be as early as 1974
but I think later makes more sense. The mock up of the screen is based on how Jones' describes
it. The logo is the one Jones made. The enemy is called mhos which is ohms backwards. He created
this based on the memory of another game so it was a little different but originally came from Chase
because it similar otherwise. Really like the orange and black. Going with the volt them next up

things all of the time. We have a bunch of version I never mentioned. This one, though, is really
weird because it is like Chase but it is also like chess. I haven't fully figured it out myself
but the idea was that the interceptor robots moved the exact same way you move. If you moved up, they
moved up which means they could never actually kill you. What did kill you was other attackers
and they moved like chess pieces I guess. I don't know. You can see a little bit of the basic code
here. It has got print commands in the middle for printing something to the screen. It has got Rays
at the bottom and so forth. Still never figured this one out. Then we have got escape with an
exclamation mark created by sub-logic for the Apple 2. Big change was it was graphics instead
of text. Played real-time and not on the grid. You can see from the graphic there some of the
things are lining up. It is more arcade that way. The player also has a gone I think for the first
time. You can zap it only eight times and you could teleport which is very popular these days.
All right. And in this one, it looks out of place here is it is totally different but there is a
bunch of games I haven't included because there was not enough light chase. I have included this
one because it was actually directly inspired by Chase and the developers of benedict. Williams

that were grunts and electrodes. That was it. When they showed it to other people they really

bunch of new enemies. They had twin shootings so you could fire off a million it seemed like zaps
all around the board and just kill everything. It was a lot of fun. All right. Next up, Zombies and
pot holes by Julian tippet 1983 for the Jupiter ace. This wasn't the first version where they

were created by tippet or someone in the computer areas that saw or adapted it. You can kind of see
it there. One interesting thing about this is a review complained that you needed eight keys to
play. People only had five fingers. Oh, my gosh, how does that work? I don't understand. Weird.
OK. Next one is a really important one mainly and this is kind of funny. This
is the one I learned how to play on. That's why I considered it important. It is hobbit
by David sweet for the TRS-80. Rainbow magazine is 1983. This is their adventure issue and he
made an adventure game. The player is supposed to be an invisible hobbit because you only see
the two eyes. The obstacles are like trees but look like mushrooms. The enemies are orcs. This

into another point here going back to who created Chase. I discovered David Sweet or
someone by the same name made a basic game back in Dartmouth college. It was about bull fighting.
It was done sometime before 1974 because it was printed in a book of in January of 1974. Is this
the same David Sweet? I don't know. Another interesting point is both games give you more

it is also possible he is the one who made the original version of Chase. We don't know that,

Robots. Very influential by Allan Black in 1984 for UNIX. It is similar to the original Chase
or the 1979 version. It doesn't come pre-stalked with obstacles -- stocked. There are no electrical

Otherwise it plays exactly the same. Then this became so well known it really became

Also had no obstacles to start until they crashed and made junk heaps. A bit of a new thing was the
sonic screwdriver. That and Daleks were part of the Doctor Who TV show. Because robots doesn't

Something abouts the logic and basicness of it. It is fun and easy to play. It is easy to
make non-violent. Zombies and pot holes didn't kill them. It is a good entry-level programming

And anything you learn how to do when you make Chase can also be applied to a roguelike later so
that's cool. You could make all sorts of genres and make changes and adapt it. Perfect example
of that is seven seas by popcap in 2001 created a pirate theme with three different types of ships.
Each worked differently. Whirlpools, treasure hunt, sea monster, all sorts of fun. Ways you

than the normal way of handling a roguelike. The monsters could be all sorts of different things
instead of just robots. Now, I kind of at the top have the three main ones here. The robot,
the zombie, and the orc. But I have a bunch of other ideas there. The enemies wouldn't have to

infect with some sort of status effect. Something like that. The electrified fences could be fields,
traps, pools of lava pits. You want to use to do whatever inspires your creativity. That's actually
it for my presentation. I don't know how I am doing on time. Questions? Things like that?

surprised how fun it is. ALEXEI: Zee cliff asks how

ALEXEI: Makes sense. There is something to say -- I read a book on a bunch of physical

carried over so many generations. DAN: That is why I think Roboton is
great because they added so much it doesn't seem like Chase but it is.
ALEXEI: Thank you, Dan, for holding out until the end and sharing this knowledge with me.
